answers.q1_what_is_it: ARCI is a CLI and Python library that runs a baseline and a candidate version of an agent many times on the same predeclared task with seeded, injected tool faults. It grades each trial with an independent oracle over the final environment state and returns PASS/BLOCK/INCONCLUSIVE/ERROR as exit code 0/1/2/3. It works like a statistical regression gate for CI, and it can also diff, minimise and replay a recorded failure offline.
answers.q2_who_for: It is for engineers who change an agent (prompt, retry policy, model, code) and want CI to catch a reliability regression before merging. A Python agent must be an importable plain function agent(task, tools, rng) -> dict that does all its tool calls through tools.call(...). You also need a toolset factory (task, seed) -> object with .tools and .snapshot() and an oracle (task, final_state) -> bool. A non-Python agent can instead be a command that speaks MCP over stdio, so ARCI's boundary sees every tool call.
answers.q3_pass_means: PASS means that for this one predeclared experiment (task, faults, seeds, N, alpha, delta), the evidence supports that the candidate's success rate is not lower than the baseline's by more than delta. Concretely, the lower bound on candidate minus baseline is above -delta. It is relative non-inferiority, not a claim that either agent is reliable in absolute terms.
answers.q4_does_not_do: It is not a sandbox or security boundary: Python agents share a process with the boundary, and a hostile agent could forge or bypass its records. It only sees calls through its tool boundary, not direct files, network or subprocesses. It replays the recorded boundary, not the model, so a live model's bundle usually replays as INVALID. Also, declaring a fault does not guarantee it fires if the agent never calls that tool.

The upper bound on the difference in success rate was below -delta (-0.10), so the gate concludes B is worse than A by more than the allowed margin, and the check fails with exit 1. answers.q1_what_is_it: ARCI is a command-line tool that tests whether a change to an AI agent made it less reliable. It runs the old agent (baseline) and the new one (candidate) many times on the same predeclared tasks, with tool faults injected on purpose. An independent check grades each run, and the tool returns PASS, BLOCK, INCONCLUSIVE or ERROR with an exit code. It can also replay a recorded failure offline.
answers.q2_who_for: It is for developers who change an agent and want a CI-style regression gate on that change. The agent can be a plain Python function agent(task, tools, rng) -> dict, or any program that speaks MCP over stdio. All its actions must go through ARCI's tool boundary, because ARCI only sees calls that cross it. For my own agent I also had to supply a toolset factory (task, seed) -> object with .tools and .snapshot(), and an oracle (task, final_state) -> bool that decides success from the end state.
answers.q3_pass_means: PASS means that, for this one predeclared experiment, the evidence supports that any reliability drop from baseline to candidate is smaller than the allowed margin (delta). Statistically, the lower bound of the confidence interval on the difference (candidate minus baseline) is above -delta. It is not a claim that the agent is reliable in absolute terms. It is relative non-inferiority only.
answers.q4_does_not_do: It is not a sandbox or security boundary: a hostile agent could forge or bypass its records. It only sees calls through the tool boundary, so files, network and subprocesses the agent touches directly are invisible. It also does not replay model inference, and a trace divergence shows where runs differ, not why. A small run is often INCONCLUSIVE.
answers.q5_first_three_commands: 1) uv tool install agent-reliability-ci. 2) arci init checkout-retry --baseline app.v1:run --candidate app.v2:run --toolset tests.world:make_world --oracle tests.world:passed. 3) arci run arci.yaml. In practice step 1 was blocked here, so I used a venv. Step 2 failed until I added --task, so my real sequence was install, init with --task, run.
answers.interpretation_demo_block: BLOCK means that in the seeded demo experiment (200 trials per arm, with a tool_timeout on reserve) agent B did measurably worse than agent A. A passed 192/200 and B passed 132/200. The upper bound of the confidence interval on the difference is below the allowed margin of -0.10, so B is worse by more than the tolerated amount. The exit code is 1, so CI would fail. The README says B is A with the retry around reserve removed, so this is a regression caught by the gate. It does not say B is bad in absolute terms.
answers.interpretation_own_run: INCONCLUSIVE (exit 2) means I did not get enough evidence either way. Both arms passed 8/8 in my 8-trial smoke run, and the interval on the difference was [-0.42, 0.42], which crosses the margin. It does not say the candidate is fine, and it does not say it regressed. The tool itself says that two perfect arms cannot PASS below N=42, so it was expected. It is not a green result and CI stays non-green. Also, my scaffold had only a clean condition with no injected fault, so it tested very little.
